sentences.text: You are a senior trainee accountant at Mthembu Inc., the audit firm appointed to audit Khanyisa Dairies Ltd for the year ended 30 September 2026.
Khanyisa processes fresh milk into pasteurised milk, yoghurt and maas at two plants in the Eastern Cape, in Gqeberha and Makhanda.
It was founded in 1987 by Themba and Grace Ndlovu, who started by collecting milk from four farms with a single truck.
Today it employs 640 people and sells about 180 million litres of dairy products a year, almost all of it in the Eastern Cape, the Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal.
Its products are sold under the Khanyisa brand, which is well known in the Eastern Cape for its yoghurt range, and under the private labels of two supermarket chains.
Revenue for the year was R2.1 billion, slightly up on the previous year, but profit after tax fell from R96 million to R41 million.
Khanyisa listed on the JSE's AltX board in 2021 to raise money for growth, but the Ndlovu family still owns 62% of the shares through the Ndlovu Family Trust.
Themba Ndlovu, now 68, is the chief executive officer and chairs the board's investment committee.
He has told the board that he plans to retire at the end of 2027, and no successor has been named.
His daughter, Lerato Ndlovu, is the operations director and is widely seen inside the company as his preferred successor.
The board has eight members, three of whom are independent non-executive directors.
One of them, Pieter van Wyk, chairs the board; he is a retired banker who joined when the company listed.
The audit committee is chaired by Ayanda Mokoena, a CA(SA) who also sits on the board of a listed retailer.
Khanyisa buys raw milk from about 120 independent dairy farmers, most of them within 150 kilometres of its plants.
It pays farmers a price per litre that is reviewed every quarter.
The Eastern Cape has had below-average rainfall for two years, and many farmers have cut the size of their herds because feed has become expensive.
As a result, Khanyisa received 9% less raw milk in 2026 than in 2025, and the Gqeberha plant ran at only 71% of its capacity for most of the year.
To keep supermarket shelves full, Khanyisa bought milk from farmers in KwaZulu-Natal at a higher price and paid more to transport it.
Management believes that supply will only recover once the drought breaks.
Two large competitors have started offering Eastern Cape farmers longer contracts at fixed prices, and eleven farmers moved to a competitor during the year.
About 45% of Khanyisa's revenue comes from one customer, the supermarket group FreshCo, which buys both Khanyisa-branded products and FreshCo's own private-label yoghurt.
The supply agreement with FreshCo ends on 31 March 2027.
FreshCo has told Khanyisa that it will renew the agreement only if Khanyisa cuts its prices by 4% and can prove that its food safety controls meet FreshCo's new standards.
The rest of the revenue comes from a second supermarket chain, independent retailers, spaza shops supplied through wholesalers, and schools and hospitals.
Sales to independent retailers grew strongly in 2026, mainly because of a popular new range of drinking yoghurts in small pouches.
In 2025 the board approved a R380 million expansion of the Makhanda plant, which will add a new long-life milk line.
Long-life milk does not need to be kept cold, so it can be sold further from the plants and exported to neighbouring countries.
The expansion is funded by a R300 million loan from Ubuntu Bank and R80 million of the company's own cash.
Construction is about seven months behind schedule because imported equipment was delayed, and the cost is now expected to reach R430 million.
The loan agreement requires Khanyisa to keep its net debt below 2.5 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.
Management expects to stay below this limit, but with little room to spare.
In June 2026, a batch of strawberry yoghurt produced at the Gqeberha plant was found to contain a harmful bacterium.
Several customers became ill, and Khanyisa recalled all yoghurt produced on the affected line over a three-week period.
The recall cost about R27 million, including the products destroyed, refunds to retailers and the cost of cleaning and testing the line.
An investigation found that a temperature sensor had failed and that the staff who checked the readings had not reported the problem.
The story was widely reported in the media, and sales of Khanyisa-branded yoghurt fell by about a fifth in the two months that followed.
Sales have since recovered to about 90% of their earlier level.
Two customers who became ill have instructed lawyers to claim damages from the company.
Most of the meeting was spent on a proposal from Themba Ndlovu to buy Amathole Cheese (Pty) Ltd, a family-owned cheese maker near Stutterheim, for about R150 million.
Themba argued that cheese would give Khanyisa a use for surplus milk in good seasons and a product with higher margins.
Two of the independent directors were against the proposal.
They said that the company should first finish the Makhanda expansion, renew the FreshCo agreement and repair its food safety reputation before taking on another business.
Pieter van Wyk also pointed out that Themba's brother-in-law owns 30% of Amathole Cheese.
The board agreed to appoint an independent adviser to value Amathole Cheese and to discuss the proposal again in January 2027.
Themba did not take part in the vote.
Gross margin fell from 24% to 19%, mainly because Khanyisa paid more for milk and transport and absorbed the cost of the recall.
Cash generated from operations fell by almost half.
The board reduced the final dividend to 20 cents a share, from 75 cents a year earlier, to keep cash for the expansion.
Debtor days rose from 38 to 47 because several wholesalers paid more slowly, and Khanyisa bought a large stock of long-life milk cartons in advance to avoid further delays once the new line starts.
The finance director, Sipho Dube, has warned the board that the company will rely on its overdraft for the next six months.
The quality control records at the Gqeberha plant are still kept on paper and are checked by shift supervisors at the end of each week.
Internal audit is outsourced to a small firm that visits twice a year.
After the recall, the board appointed a food safety consultancy to review controls at both plants; its report is due in December 2026.
Khanyisa also plans to replace its accounting system in 2027, as the current system cannot record batch costs for each product line.
Management's plan for 2027 is to start the long-life milk line, export to Botswana and Namibia, renew the FreshCo agreement and launch the pouch yoghurt range in the Western Cape.
It also intends to appoint a head of food safety who reports directly to the audit committee.
Khanyisa installed solar panels at both plants in 2025, which now supply about a third of their electricity and have reduced the impact of power cuts.
The company's B-BBEE rating matters to several of its public sector customers, and it is due for reassessment in February 2027.
The human resources department reports high staff turnover among qualified food technologists, because larger food companies in Gauteng pay more.

recall.question: What kind of business is Khanyisa?
options: A dairy processor that sells mainly to supermarkets

recall.question: What is your role?
options: A trainee at the firm that audits Khanyisa
An adviser on the cheese deal

recall.question: Who controls Khanyisa?
options: The Ndlovu family, through a trust

recall.question: Why is Khanyisa getting less milk?
options: Drought has made farmers cut their herds, and some farmers left for competitors

recall.question: Which customer relationship is at risk?
options: The agreement with its largest supermarket customer
Its contracts with schools and hospitals

recall.question: What went wrong during the year?
options: Contaminated yoghurt led to a product recall
The company failed a tax audit

recall.question: How is the plant expansion going?
What was the board meeting mainly about?
options: A proposal to buy a cheese maker

recall.question: What is the main plan for 2027?
options: Start the long-life milk line and begin exporting

recall.question: Why did some directors object to that proposal?
options: Bad timing given other pressures, and the CEO's family has an interest in the seller
The seller is outside South Africa
The bank refused to fund it
